title: Why NATO and the Transatlantic Bond Will Outlast Trump | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Kupchan argues that despite Trump's dismissiveness toward NATO, aid cuts to Ukraine, and Greenland threats, a transatlantic rupture is highly unlikely because enduring common interests bind the two—Russia's war makes quitting Europe strategic folly, and over $2 trillion in annual transatlantic trade reinforces the bond. Trump's pressure is working: nearly all NATO members agreed to 5 percent of GDP defense spending by 2035. But European strategic autonomy 'isn't happening'—capability gaps take a decade to fill and members won't pool sovereignty.

insights.claim: Trump's dismissive attitude toward NATO, his decision to turn off aid to Ukraine, his threats to seize Greenland from Denmark, and his attack on Iran give Europeans reason to doubt the U.S. alliance, but Kupchan judges an irreparable rupture highly unlikely.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: A CFR/Georgetown analyst arguing against transatlantic breakup pushes back on the consensus rupture narrative—relevant for European defense and Ukraine-exposed positioning.
insights.quote: Yet it is far too soon to pronounce the irreparable rupture and death of the transatlantic alliance.

insights.claim: Europe needs a plan B for self-reliance in case the impulsive and unpredictable Trump decides to pull the plug and leave NATO, but that outcome is highly unlikely because the alliance rests on enduring common interests and values.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: Base case is NATO endures and is fortified; European self-reliance prep is a hedge, not the central scenario.
insights.quote: It is quite likely that NATO will emerge from the Trump era not only intact but fortified by a strengthened European pillar.
insights.locator: But that outcome is highly unlikely.

insights.claim: Trump's pressure campaign, coupled with a resurgent Russian threat, is working: nearly all NATO members have agreed to spend 5 percent of GDP on armed forces and security infrastructure by 2035.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: A 5%-of-GDP-by-2035 commitment across nearly all members is a durable multi-year tailwind for European defense spending and contractors.
insights.quote: Nearly all NATO members have agreed to spend 5 percent of GDP on their armed forces and security infrastructure by 2035.
insights.locator: But coupled with a resurgent Russian threat

insights.claim: Germany, Europe's largest economy, has built a solid political consensus behind major investments in its military establishment.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: German political consensus for rearmament is the anchor of the European defense-spend cycle—watch German procurement as the bellwether.
insights.locator: It is particularly important that Germany

insights.claim: The Pentagon is undertaking a force posture review that could lead to downsizing the U.S. military presence in Europe, even as Trump continues to call allies 'delinquent.'
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: A force-posture review is the concrete mechanism for a possible U.S. drawdown in Europe—a catalyst to monitor for European defense gaps.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, the Pentagon is undertaking a force posture review

themes.theme: Why the bond still serves the U.S.

insights.claim: Kupchan argues it would be strategic folly for the U.S. to quit Europe while Russia's war against Ukraine continues, because U.S. forces are still needed to deter Russian aggression and forward bases in Europe let the U.S. project power into Africa, the Middle East, and beyond.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: The U.S. self-interest case (deterrence plus power projection) is the structural reason to expect continuity in the alliance despite the rhetoric.
insights.quote: Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine and Moscow's threatening posture toward NATO's eastern flank would make it an act of strategic folly for the United States to quit Europe.
insights.locator: Yet Trump is quite unlikely to walk away

insights.claim: Transatlantic trade in goods and services tops $2 trillion per year and more than one thousand flights crisscross the Atlantic every day during summer, reinforcing the strategic bond with economic and societal linkages.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: Over $2 trillion in annual trade is ballast that raises the cost of any real rupture—supporting the continuity base case.
insights.quote: Transatlantic trade in goods and services tops $2 trillion per year.
insights.locator: Vibrant transatlantic trade, investment, and tourism

insights.claim: Even with impressive committed spending increases, it will take a decade or more for new European expenditures to fill significant military capability gaps, so Europe will continue to need U.S. manpower, firepower, lift, and intelligence in the meantime.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: Europe's dependence on U.S. capabilities persists for a decade-plus regardless of budgets—autonomy is a long-horizon, not near-term, trade.
insights.quote: it will take a decade or more for new expenditures to fill significant gaps in military capability

insights.claim: The British and French nuclear arsenals are small and limited in capability and do not match the deterrent punch of the U.S. nuclear umbrella, even as Paris floats extending France's nuclear umbrella to its neighbors.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: No credible European nuclear substitute exists—Europe cannot afford a strategic divorce from the U.S. while facing Russia.
insights.locator: Britain and France do have nuclear weapons

insights.claim: Europe's strategic deficit is political: member states remain reluctant to pool sovereignty over war and peace, and growing populist and ethnonationalist parties are fueling anti-EU forces that make shifting security authority to Brussels even harder.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: Rising populism structurally blocks the political unification needed for autonomy—so Europe will keep punching below its weight and leaning on the U.S.
insights.quote: the growing strength of populist parties and ethnonationalism is fueling anti-EU forces
insights.locator: Europe's strategic deficit is also political

insights.claim: Kupchan concludes that passionate calls for European strategic autonomy sound good but it 'is not happening,' because the U.S. still needs Europe and Europe still needs the U.S.—a reality that will not change soon.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: Bet on continued mutual dependence, not a clean European autonomy story—shapes expectations for NATO durability and defense-industrial demand.
insights.quote: Passionate calls for Europe's strategic autonomy sound good, but it's not happening.
insights.locator: Passionate calls for Europe's strategic autonomy
